Moral Foundations Theory is a framework that separates human morality into the following categories:

  - Care/Harm: related to our long evolution as mammals with attachment systems
    and an ability to feel (and dislike) the pain of others. It underlies the
    virtues of kindness, gentleness, and nurturance.

  - Loyalty/Betrayal: related to our long history as tribal creatures able to
    form shifting coalitions. It is active anytime people feel that it is "one
    for all and all for one." It underlies the virtues of patriotism and
    self-sacrifice for the group.

  - Authority/Subversion: shaped by our long primate history of hierarchical
    social interactions. It underlies virtues of leadership and followership,
    including deference to prestigious authority figures and respect for
    traditions.

  - Sanctity/Purity: shaped by the psychology of disgust and contamination. It
    underlies notions of striving to live in an elevated, less carnal, more
    noble, and more "natural" way (often present in religious narratives). This
    foundation underlies the widespread idea that the body is a temple that can
    be desecrated by immoral activities and contaminants (an idea not unique to
    religious traditions). It underlies the virtues of self-discipline,
    self-improvement, naturalness, and spirituality.

  - Equality: related to our intuitions about equal treatment and equal outcome
    for individuals.

  - Proportionality: related to our intuitions about individuals getting
    rewarded in proportion to their merit or contribution.

# Conservative Party Manifesto 2024: Summary

## Economic Policy

The manifesto outlines plans to reduce National Insurance from 12% to 6% by April 2027, representing a £1,350 annual reduction for average workers earning £35,000. Self-employed individuals would see complete abolition of the main rate of National Insurance by Parliament's end. The party commits to maintaining fiscal rules requiring public sector net debt to fall and borrowing to remain below 3% of GDP.

For businesses, the manifesto proposes maintaining corporation tax rates, extending "full expensing" to leasing when conditions allow, and implementing a ten-point plan for SMEs including business rates relief and improved access to finance.

## Migration and Borders

The manifesto proposes introducing a legally binding annual cap on migration covering work and family visas, with Parliament voting on levels each year. Salary thresholds for Skilled Worker visas have increased to £38,700. Regarding illegal migration, the plan includes removal flights to Rwanda, clearing asylum backlogs within six months, and working internationally to reform asylum treaties.

## Public Services

NHS spending would increase above inflation annually, with recruitment of 92,000 additional nurses and 28,000 doctors. The manifesto outlines 250 new or modernised GP surgeries, 50 additional Community Diagnostic Centres, and expansion of Pharmacy First services.

For education, the document proposes the Advanced British Standard for 16-19 education, mandatory National Service for 18-year-olds (either military or civic), and 100,000 additional apprenticeships funded by reducing university courses deemed to have poor outcomes.

## Housing and Infrastructure

Targets include 1.6 million new homes in England, with measures to unlock brownfield development and protect Green Belt. First-time buyers would receive permanent Stamp Duty relief up to £425,000 and access to a new Help to Buy scheme.

Transport investment totals £36 billion from HS2 savings, including £8.3 billion for road maintenance and funding for Northern Powerhouse Rail between Manchester and Liverpool.

## Energy and Environment

The manifesto commits to net zero by 2050 while pledging annual oil and gas licensing rounds in the North Sea and no new green levies on household bills. Plans include trebling offshore wind capacity, building carbon capture clusters, and expanding nuclear power including Small Modular Reactors.

## Defence and Foreign Policy

Defence spending would increase to 2.5% of GDP by 2030, with at least £10 billion invested in domestic munitions production over the decade. The manifesto confirms continued support for Ukraine and maintenance of the nuclear deterrent.

# Summary of the Labour Party Manifesto 2024

## Overview and Approach

The Labour Party's 2024 manifesto presents a programme for government centered on five key missions: economic growth, clean energy, public safety, educational opportunity, and NHS reform. The document emphasizes economic stability, public service improvement, and institutional reform.

## Economic Policy

Labour proposes strict fiscal rules requiring the current budget to balance and debt to fall as a share of the economy by the forecast's fifth year. The party commits to capping corporation tax at 25%, maintaining full expensing for capital investment, and reforming business rates. A National Wealth Fund would be established with £7.3 billion to invest in ports, manufacturing, and green industries.

The manifesto outlines an industrial strategy featuring a statutory Industrial Strategy Council, sector-specific plans for automotive, life sciences, and creative industries, and planning system reforms. Labour pledges to build 1.5 million new homes through updated planning frameworks, brownfield-first development, strategic greenbelt release, and new towns.

On taxation, the party commits to not increasing income tax, National Insurance, or VAT, while abolishing non-domicile tax status and closing private equity carried interest loopholes.

## Energy and Environment

Labour plans to achieve clean power by 2030 through doubling onshore wind, tripling solar, and quadrupling offshore wind. Great British Energy, a new publicly-owned company capitalized at £8.3 billion, would invest in clean energy projects. The manifesto includes a £6.6 billion Warm Homes Plan for home insulation upgrades.

Regarding oil and gas, Labour would not issue new exploration licenses but would manage existing fields for their lifespan and extend the Energy Profits Levy while removing investment allowances.

## Public Services

For the NHS, Labour pledges 40,000 additional weekly appointments, doubled CT/MRI scanners, 8,500 new mental health staff, and reforms to dentistry access. The party proposes shifting toward community-based care and prevention.

On policing, the manifesto outlines a Neighbourhood Policing Guarantee with additional officers, new antisocial behaviour powers, and measures to halve knife crime within a decade.

Education reforms include 6,500 new teachers funded by ending private school tax exemptions, 3,000 new primary school nurseries, free breakfast clubs, curriculum review, and Skills England to coordinate training.

## Immigration and Borders

Labour proposes a Border Security Command with counter-terrorism powers to address irregular migration, additional caseworkers to clear asylum backlogs, ending hotel accommodation for asylum seekers, and linking immigration policy with domestic skills training.

## Constitutional and Governance Reform

The manifesto includes removing hereditary peers from the House of Lords, introducing a mandatory retirement age of 80 for peers, establishing an Ethics and Integrity Commission, extending voting rights to 16-17 year olds, and creating a Council of Nations and Regions.

## Foreign Policy and Defence

Labour commits to NATO, the nuclear deterrent, and a Strategic Defence Review. The party pledges to improve EU relations through a veterinary agreement and mutual recognition of professional qualifications without rejoining the single market or customs union. The manifesto maintains support for Ukraine and commits to recognizing Palestinian statehood.

## Funding

Revenue measures include windfall tax extensions on oil and gas companies, non-dom status abolition, private equity tax reform, private school VAT, and efficiency savings across government.
